prerequisites: Basic knowledge of physics and mathematics is recommended.

learning_outcomes.text: understand how sound is generated, propagated, and perceived
be able to measure, visualize, and interpret acoustic and vibration signals
understand the role of time-domain analysis and convolution in signal processing
be able to assess environmental noise and acoustic comfort
apply basic principles of noise control, sound absorption, and sound insulation
gain introductory experience in sound event classification and data-driven analysis
develop the ability to connect physical measurements with human perception and context

syllabus_topics: Introduction to sound perception and perception of different sound environments
Experimental methods for sound measurement and evaluation of human response
Digital signal processing: FFT, convolution, signal differentiation and integration
Time–frequency representations and transient sound analysis
Noise control measures using sound absorption and sound insulation
Introduction to artificial intelligence in acoustics: sound event classification based on feature extraction, supervised (k-NN) and unsupervised (K-Means) methods
Case studies from real environments and machines (urban soundscapes, machinery, transport, nature)

assessment_methods.method: Group oral presentation with peer self-assessment
Evaluation of group performance during experimental work

bibliography: Thomas D. Rossing, “Springer Handbook of Acoustics”, Springer 2007, LLC New York
David M. Howard & Jamie A.S. Angus, “Acoustics and Psychoacoustics”, Focal Press 2009, Oxford
degree: Mechanical Engineering (2nd cycle, Erasmus+ subjects, Research and Development programme)
